sub_claim: On the evening of Wednesday 18 November the President, serenaded at his lodging, answered the crowd with a short refusal to speak, which five papers print in three wordings (the Tribune and the Herald print one text). The Evening Star and the Daily National Republican (20 Nov) print "I appear before you, fellow-citizens, merely to thank you for this compliment", "The most substantial of these is that I have no speech to make [laughter.] It is somewhat important in my position that one should not say any foolish things if he can help it, and it very often happens that the only way to help it is to say nothing at all. [Renewed laughter.] Believing that that is my precise position this evening, I must beg of you to excuse me from saying 'one word.'" and "The President was most enthusiastically greeted, and when he retired, he did so amid prolonged applause." The New-York Tribune (20 Nov) prints "After supper the President was serenaded by the excellent band of the 5th New-York Artillery" and, in a different wording, "In my position it is somewhat important that I should not say any foolish things. A VOICE—If you can help it. Mr. LINCOLN—It very often happens that the only way to help it is to say nothing at all. [Laughter.] Believing that is my present condition this evening, I must beg of you to excuse me from addressing you further. The President retired amid loud cheers." The New York Herald (20 Nov) prints the same wording as the Tribune ("In my position it is somewhat important that I should not say any foolish things. A VOICE—If you can help it. Mr. LINCOLN—It very often happens that the only way to help it is to say nothing at all (Laughter.)") and "The President retired amidst loud cheers"; the Richmond Daily Dispatch (24 Nov), summarising a description printed by the New York Herald, prints "Lincoln was serenaded the night preceding the day on which the ceremony took place" and that he "declined to make a speech".

sub_claim: On the evening of Wednesday 18 November the President, serenaded at his lodging, answered the crowd with a short refusal to speak, which five papers print in three wordings (the Tribune and the Herald print one text). The Evening Star and the Daily National Republican (20 Nov) print "I appear before you, fellow-citizens, merely to thank you for this compliment", "The most substantial of these is that I have no speech to make [laughter.] It is somewhat important in my position that one should not say any foolish things if he can help it, and it very often happens that the only way to help it is to say nothing at all. [Renewed laughter.] Believing that that is my precise position this evening, I must beg of you to excuse me from saying 'one word.'" and "The President was most enthusiastically greeted, and when he retired, he did so amid prolonged applause." The New-York Tribune (20 Nov) prints "After supper the President was serenaded by the excellent band of the 5th New-York Artillery" and, in a different wording, "In my position it is somewhat important that I should not say any foolish things. A VOICE—If you can help it. Mr. LINCOLN—It very often happens that the only way to help it is to say nothing at all. [Laughter.] Believing that is my present condition this evening, I must beg of you to excuse me from addressing you further. The President retired amid loud cheers." The New York Herald (20 Nov) prints the same wording as the Tribune ("In my position it is somewhat important that I should not say any foolish things. A VOICE—If you can help it. Mr. LINCOLN—It very often happens that the only way to help it is to say nothing at all (Laughter.)") and "The President retired amidst loud cheers"; the Richmond Daily Dispatch (24 Nov), summarising a description printed by the New York Herald, prints "Lincoln was serenaded the night preceding the day on which the ceremony took place" and that he "declined to make a speech".
